lessons.title: Outbreaks, epidemics and historical impact
lessons.goal: Use time, place and population evidence to distinguish an outbreak, epidemic and pandemic, then compare historical disease cases fairly.
lessons.before: Chapter 9 distinguished an infectious agent from its transmission route and the conditions that affect exposure.
lessons.openingTitle: A school cluster is not automatically a pandemic
opening: Several students in one school become ill in a week. Health staff first ask whether the cases are linked, when symptoms began and whether the number exceeds what is expected. The word pandemic requires a much wider geographic pattern; it cannot be inferred from the seriousness of one local cluster.

Historical disease stories also need context. An organism may be introduced into a population with limited prior exposure while displacement, crowding, nutrition, care access and colonial policies shape consequences. Avoid treating Indigenous peoples as a single biological group or attributing harm to one simple cause.
lessons.mechanismTitle: Compare scale with a dated record
mechanism: An outbreak is a cluster of cases above what is expected in a defined place and period. An epidemic is a larger-than-expected pattern in a population or region; a pandemic is an epidemic spread across multiple countries or continents. These are public-health descriptions of spread, not a ranking of how severe every individual case is.

The workbook's plague, tuberculosis, 1918 influenza and AIDS table asks for social conditions, impact, time and place. Use dates and sources for each row. A single chart cannot prove that a disease acted identically in every region or that present-day services are the same as those of an earlier era.

workedExamples.title: Classify a local cluster carefully
workedExamples.situation: A town records 25 cases in one week when it normally sees about two.
steps: Define the period and population before comparing 25 with about two.
Treat the excess as an outbreak signal that deserves investigation; identify likely links and reporting quality.
Do not call it a pandemic without evidence of sustained international spread.
workedExamples.interpretation: The classification depends on the pattern and scale, not only the count or the illness name.

workedExamples.title: Compare two historical records
workedExamples.situation: A textbook gives a 1918 influenza death total and a later national disease rate.
steps: Record each source's year, geography and measure: total deaths and rate are different units.
Convert or locate comparable measures before ranking impact.
Explain the social setting and uncertainty, including access to reporting and care.
workedExamples.interpretation: Historical comparisons are strongest when their measures and context are stated explicitly.

terms: outbreak
More cases than expected in a defined place and time.
An unusual cluster at one school can trigger an investigation.
It does not by itself mean worldwide spread.
epidemic
An increase above expected cases across a population or region.
A regional rise over several weeks may be an epidemic.
Severity and geographic spread are different questions.
pandemic
An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.
The 1918 influenza pandemic affected many regions.
A single local outbreak is not a pandemic.
historical context
The time, place, social conditions and evidence needed to interpret a past event.
Compare 1918 reports with the care and reporting available then.
A dated figure is not automatically a current statistic.
lessons.transferPrompt: A news post calls one city's disease cluster a pandemic. Write what evidence would support a local outbreak description and what additional evidence would be needed for pandemic language.
lessons.transferModel: A local increase above expected cases during a stated period could support an outbreak. Pandemic language requires evidence of sustained spread across multiple countries or continents, using comparable surveillance data.
lessons.laterPrompt: From memory, explain why case count alone cannot distinguish outbreak, epidemic and pandemic, and name two context fields for a historical comparison.
lessons.laterModel: The expected baseline, population, time and geographic extent are needed. Historical records should include date, location and measure, such as deaths or cases per population.

lessons.title: Public systems for water, waste and air
lessons.goal: Trace how community monitoring and treatment reduce exposure through water, waste and air pathways.
lessons.before: Lesson 6 showed that disease patterns are measured over time and that a community response involves more than one household.
lessons.openingTitle: A clear glass does not prove safe water
opening: A glass of tap water looks clear. Appearance alone cannot show whether a harmful microorganism or chemical is present. The source, treatment, distribution system and monitoring records together support a safety judgment.

Public health operates through shared systems: drinking-water standards and sampling, waste collection and treatment, food inspection, disease surveillance and air alerts. Responsibilities vary by jurisdiction and can change, so the older workbook's agency names should be read as historical examples rather than a permanent directory.
lessons.mechanismTitle: Trace each pathway to a control point
mechanism: Water may become contaminated at the source or during distribution. Testing can detect an indicator or contaminant, treatment can reduce hazards, and a warning can protect people while a system is repaired. Landfills and wastewater facilities are designed to reduce leakage and exposure; design and operation matter, so a liner alone is not proof of no risk.

Air monitoring detects conditions that may increase health risk. An alert communicates a recommended response for a specified place and time. The CBE archive's older index table and the workbook's fixed number bands should not be presented as current AQHI guidance; check a current local authority for today's advice.

workedExamples.title: Follow a drinking-water failure
workedExamples.situation: A routine sample detects a contamination indicator at one point in a water system.
steps: Locate the sample and determine what the test actually measured.
Investigate possible source, treatment or distribution failure and repeat/confirm tests as directed.
Communicate an appropriate precaution while the operator and health authority investigate and correct the pathway.
workedExamples.interpretation: A response combines detection, communication and repair. One clear glass or one negative sample cannot describe the entire system.

workedExamples.title: Read an air alert without inventing a threshold
workedExamples.situation: A local air-quality notice advises some people to reduce strenuous outdoor activity.
steps: Identify the issuing authority, location, date and pollutant or index named.
Read the advice for the relevant risk group rather than applying an old workbook number band.
Explain that monitoring estimates exposure risk; the notice does not diagnose each individual.
workedExamples.interpretation: A current alert is a decision aid tied to current monitoring and local guidance.

terms: water treatment
Processes used to reduce hazards in drinking water before distribution.
Filtration and disinfection may be parts of a treatment system.
Clear appearance alone does not show effective treatment.
surveillance
Systematic collection and interpretation of health or environmental information.
Regular water samples can reveal a changing pattern.
One observation is not a complete trend.
wastewater
Used water containing human or other wastes that needs management.
A community treatment plant reduces release of harmful material.
It is not the same as untreated drinking water.
public advisory
A time- and place-specific notice that recommends protective action.
A water or air notice may guide temporary behaviour.
It is not an individual diagnosis.
lessons.transferPrompt: A community receives both a drinking-water warning and an air-quality notice. For each, name the pathway, one measurement or observation, one system-level action and one limit of the evidence.
lessons.transferModel: For water, sampling may indicate contamination; treatment repair and a temporary warning address ingestion risk, but one sample cannot map the whole network. For air, monitors support a local advisory; emission controls or activity advice may reduce exposure, but the notice does not predict one person's illness.
lessons.laterPrompt: Without looking, write the sequence source → monitoring → control → communication for a drinking-water example.
lessons.laterModel: A water source is sampled, test results are interpreted, treatment or distribution problems are corrected, and the public receives a timely advisory when needed.

lessons.title: Guidelines, risk decisions and the Walkerton case
lessons.goal: Use a source timeline to identify warning signs, system failures and justified prevention decisions.
lessons.before: Lesson 7 traced how monitoring, treatment and communication work together in a public system.
lessons.openingTitle: When a warning sign is missed
opening: A town's water safety depends on more than a treatment device. Sampling, accurate records, trained operators, oversight and clear communication must all function. The Walkerton case is a source-based way to investigate how a chain can fail, without pretending one person's choice explains every consequence.

The workbook cites textbook printed p. 186 for its timeline, but p. 186 is missing from the supplied PDF. Use the original workbook p. 16 prompt and any teacher-supplied timeline. The online lesson must state this gap rather than invent the missing page.
lessons.mechanismTitle: Turn a case into an evidence-based recommendation
mechanism: A risk table separates a factor, a concern and a response. Population density may make contact and monitoring needs different; travel and migration can change where an infection is detected; food handling and water distribution create distinct control points. None of these factors makes a group of people inherently dangerous.

In a case analysis, first put events in time order. Then connect each warning sign to a control that could have detected, prevented or limited harm. Distinguish what the provided timeline establishes from a hypothesis that would require additional records. A public-health guideline is useful when its mechanism, evidence and practical instructions are clear.

workedExamples.title: Complete one risk-table row
workedExamples.situation: The workbook lists a growing community and asks for a concern and a response.
steps: State the concern: more people can increase demand on water, waste and disease-monitoring systems.
Link a response to that mechanism: scale sampling, staffing and emergency communication to the larger population.
Avoid claiming population growth itself is a pathogen or guarantees an outbreak.
workedExamples.interpretation: A good table cell explains how a response addresses the named concern.

workedExamples.title: Evaluate a timeline claim
workedExamples.situation: A timeline shows an adverse test result followed by a delayed public warning.
steps: Record the two events and their dates exactly as shown.
Ask which records would show when the result was received and who had authority to act.
Propose a control: an escalation rule that connects a confirmed result to prompt review and communication.
workedExamples.interpretation: The timeline supports a concern about response delay; assigning individual fault requires more evidence.

terms: risk assessment
A structured comparison of hazards, exposure, likelihood and possible consequences.
A water operator assesses a positive sample and possible users exposed.
A hazard name alone is not a complete risk estimate.
public-health guideline
A recommendation or rule intended to reduce a stated population health risk.
A sampling and notification protocol guides water-system action.
A guideline should be tied to mechanism and evidence.
warning sign
An observation that calls for investigation or action.
An unexpected test result can be a warning sign.
It is not necessarily a final diagnosis of the whole system.
escalation
Passing a concern to the person or authority able to act, following a defined process.
A confirmed test result triggers timely review and public notice when appropriate.
Recording a concern without action is not complete escalation.
lessons.transferPrompt: Using the original Walkerton workbook task or a teacher-provided timeline, choose one warning sign, one missed or effective control, and one recommendation. Mark any claim that requires evidence beyond the timeline.
lessons.transferModel: A positive water test is a warning sign. A clear rule for confirming, escalating and communicating the result can limit exposure. A timeline alone may not show what every worker knew at the time, so an individual-blame claim needs additional records.
lessons.laterPrompt: From memory, explain how to turn a risk factor into a justified public-health response without blaming a group.
lessons.laterModel: Name the exposure pathway and the system weakness, then choose a control that interrupts it. Assess the action with evidence; do not label people as the hazard.
